chapter: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
title: Mutt sues a restaurant that refused service
summary: At a Paramount lunch spot, light-skinned Joe and Ram were served but Mutt and L.Z. Cooper were refused, and Mutt sued and won about five hundred dollars.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That particular was the one you heard me tell about where they had... They had so much bigotry here in Los Angeles, and prejudice.
Darensbourg - 159
I know all about that stuff in the South, but I didn't realize it was all out here, too.

Actually, right at the Paramount Studio, that same studio up on Melrose now, they had this little old bitty restaurant across the street, where when you got a break for lunch... They didn't have a studio commissary in those days; at least I didn't see any in Paramount Studios. So everybody would go across the street at this restaurant. L.Z. Cooper was in the band at the time, and Papa Mutt, and I can't think who else. But I know Ram and I, Minor Hall, we still had these straw hats on, and we walked across there, and naturally Ram was real light-colored, and me -- they didn't know whether we was Black, Indian or anything else. They just flat-out served us, although they didn't serve Black people at that time. They used to have little signs: 'We reserve the right to refuse service to anyone.' But anyway, me and Ram are sitting right there inside, eating, and here come L.Z. Cooper and Papa Mutt, you see. And the waitress kept passing them by, and meantime me and Ram was eatin'... [LAUGHS] So Papa Mutt says, 'What the hell is this waitress...?' So finally, 'Why don't you come wait on us?' Finally he called, 'Hey, miss, me and this fellow here want to get some service.' And she says, 'I'm sorry, we don't serve colored people in here.' And Ram whispers
Darensbourg - 160

over to L.Z. Cooper and says, "Get the hell up from here; you'll get me and Joe in trouble. Don't sit next to me!" Honest to God! And Papa Mutt started whooping and hollering: "Get me a piece of paper. I want to write these guys... Oh, everybody's a witness. Write your name and address down."
Well, what could he have done?
Well, he could sue them.
Is that right?
Yes, sir, if you've got witnesses.
How did that work, because in Louisiana it was state law that....
No, it wasn't a state law here, though. People just took it on themselves...
So it was supposed to be desegregated...
Well, all the schools were desegregated. They never had any segregation laws here. Not in Los Angeles.
I didn't know that.
And people, Southerners or whoever it was, came up here and took it on themselves not to serve Colored people or Black people. And I think Mutt got five hundred dollars out of it.
Oh, he did sue them.
Darensbourg - 161
Yes, sir.

So it must have been a strange situation for someone like Mutt and Ram and them, coming up from New Orleans and finding all this... I mean, in New Orleans you couldn't sue anybody for that. You just had to take it on the chin, and that was that.
Oh, Los Angeles was a very segregated town at that time, believe me.
But I mean, the very fact that Mutt could sue a restaurant. In the South it was really...

That's right. It just goes to show you what... They had passed that law if somebody don't serve you, provided you got witnesses, you can sue them...I think five dollars was tops. So a lot of guys just didn't abide by the law, figured they'd get away with it -- which they did. But Mutt didn't let them do that.
